description: We’re Cosmosen, a team of 2: Tomás Ávila and Facundo Gonzalez, from Buenos Aires. We’re here at Space Apps to build something that actually works in 48 hours, not just an idea on paper: a prototype that turns NASA’s open data into something useful, with a clear vision and a solid demo.
summary: Cosmosen (RaHel) turns an ordinary Wear OS smartwatch into a continuous vital-signs monitor for people working far from medical support, such as astronauts, remote field crews and isolated teams. A Wear OS app reads heart rate and steps once per second, keeps working with the screen off through a health foreground service, stores readings offline and syncs them securely to a web dashboard linked with a one-time code. The server estimates what the watch does not measure (heart rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep and stress) from the received heart-rate and step history, always labeled as estimated with a confidence level, so measured and estimated data are never mixed. A batch AI analysis page, enabled only with user consent, summarizes trends. A public demo mode with simulated data lets anyone try the full dashboard without a watch. It matters because long-duration missions and remote work need low-cost, continuous health awareness using hardware people already wear.
details:
Repository to Github: Rahel

https://github.com/VMASPAD/rahel

WHAT IT DOES

Cosmosen (RaHel) is an end-to-end remote health-monitoring system: a Wear OS watch app, a backend, and a web dashboard.

- Watch app (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose for Wear OS): reads heart rate and steps every second, runs an on-watch wellbeing assessment, and keeps recording with the screen off using a health foreground service with an ongoing activity. Readings are queued locally, so nothing is lost without connection, and are uploaded in batches without duplicates. It includes a tile and a complication.

- Pairing: the watch shows a one-time code that the user types in the web dashboard. Codes expire and have attempt limits; each device gets its own token.

- Backend (Node.js, Express, TypeScript, SQLite): validates every payload, stores the time series and serves the dashboard. It estimates heart rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep and stress from the received heart-rate and step history, resampled over a 24-hour window. Estimates are labeled "estimated" with a confidence level; skin temperature is never invented.

- Web dashboard (React, Vite, Tailwind): live and historical view per watch, sensor analytics (which fields arrive, coverage, measured vs. estimated) and an Analysis page that sends data to an AI service for batch summaries, only with explicit consent.

- Demo mode: a fully separate simulator with deterministic fake data and simulated AI answers, so judges can try everything without a watch and without any network call to the real API.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Missions far from Earth and remote operations need continuous, low-cost health awareness. Our approach uses hardware people already wear, shares data with the team only through an explicit pairing step, and is transparent about what is measured and what is estimated. It is not a medical device and its output is indicative.

TOOLS

Kotlin, Jetpack Compose for Wear OS, Wear Tiles and Complications, Health Services permissions; Node.js, Express, TypeScript, SQLite (better-sqlite3), zod, JWT; React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Router, React Bits components (animated UI). Hardware tested: a Samsung Galaxy Watch (Wear OS).

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS

Separating measured from estimated data, offline-first sync, consent-gated AI analysis and a no-hardware demo mode. We considered privacy (pairing codes, per-account access, data deletion on request), battery use and the limits of optical heart-rate sensing.

RELEVANCE TO THE CHALLENGE

This project responds to "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". On long missions astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in their own health. Cosmosen (RaHel) gathers cardiovascular and activity indicators from a wearable, shows the astronaut an on-device wellbeing assessment, and gives the crew a dashboard with history, sensor analytics and consent-gated AI summaries, so they can evaluate and act on their status. We focus on cardiovascular and behavioral-health signals (heart rate, resting heart rate, sleep and stress estimates). It does not address radiation, bone or immune effects, and it has not been validated with spaceflight data or against a clinical reference: the NASA study we cite (ISS Bluetooth heart-rate monitors vs. 12-lead ECG) defines the ±5 bpm yardstick we plan to use.



SI DISCLOSURE

Code, documentation and copy in this project were developed with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant, under the team's direction and review. The idea, the product concept and the decisions are the team's. The batch analysis feature calls an external AI service (TypeSafe AI) only with user consent. No NASA branding was generated, used or modified.
